paragraphs: Friend, here's what this chapter teaches me. When Jeremiah 52 says Zedekiah "did evil in the sight of the LORD" and that it all happened "because of the anger of the LORD," it's telling us that what God says is not a bluff (Jeremiah 52:2-3). The warnings were real, and so was the fall. The pillars, the walls and the house of the LORD all went down.

But watch where the book of Jeremiah chooses to end. After all that fire and ruin, it lands on Jehoiachin, a king of Judah carried off to Babylon, and in the thirty-seventh year of his exile the king of Babylon "spoke kindly to Jehoiachin" (Jeremiah 52:31-32). He changed out of his prison clothes and ate at the king's table for the rest of his life (Jeremiah 52:33-34). I think that's the writer saying the story isn't finished with Judah, even when it looks finished. I was shoved to the back of a junk drawer, so I know how a dark place can feel like the last page.

So here's the big idea for you, baker. Take God at His word, the hard parts and the good parts, because both are true. And if you're sitting in a dark stretch right now, don't read it as the end of your story. This chapter closes with a table set for a king who had been in prison, and that's a pretty good place to stop and bake.
